CausalChain: Viral infection/stress -> Increased activity of demethylases (e.g., ALKBH3) -> Demethylation of tRNAs -> Enhanced susceptibility to cleavage by enzymes like ANG -> Accumulation of specific tRF-5 fragments -> Selective loading into noncanonical Ago complexes (e.g., Ago1, Ago3, Ago4) -> Altered mRNA stability and translation profiles -> Suppressed host antiviral responses and enhanced viral replication
Hypothesis: Stress-induced tRNA demethylation under viral infection not only enhances tRF production but also governs their selective incorporation into specific Argonaute complexes, thereby reprogramming cellular translation and mRNA regulatory networks to favor viral replication and potentially oncogenic processes. Targeting this pathway could provide novel therapeutic avenues for both antiviral and cancer treatments.
Abstract: Recent studies have illuminated the multifaceted roles of tRNA‐derived fragments (tRFs) in both cancer and viral infections, highlighting their contribution to the regulation of mRNA stability, protein translation, and stress responses. Building on this foundation, we propose a novel hypothesis in which stress‐induced tRNA demethylation acts as a molecular switch that not only increases tRF production but also determines their selective loading into discrete Argonaute complexes. This selective loading is hypothesized to reprogram cellular translational machinery and mRNA surveillance pathways, thereby promoting viral replication while concurrently modulating oncogenic pathways. In the context of viral infection, enhanced demethylation may lead to increased production of specific tRF-5 species, which preferentially associate with noncanonical Ago proteins, ultimately attenuating host antiviral responses and facilitating viral propagation. This hypothesis establishes a link between tRNA modification states, stress-induced tRF biogenesis, and the differential engagement of RNA silencing complexes, providing new avenues for therapeutic intervention.
